newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP to back labelling rules for dangerous products.
newsitem.headline: EP to back labelling rules for dangerous products.

text.p: The European Parliament is due on Thursday to approve plans to put clearer, more detailed warning labels on thousands of carcinogenic or poisonous substances and other dangerous products.

Over the years, the European Union has made numerous piecemeal attempts to standardise its member states' laws on classifying, packaging and labelling hazardous preparations, to ensure that users in all 15 EU countries receive equally detailed product safety information.
The result is a pile of different pieces of legislation, some relating to pure chemicals, others to preparations composed of two or more chemical substances, and a third set relating to pesticides.

Now the European Commission is proposing to bring all these laws together in a single binding directive, which will also update and extend the labelling requirements manufacturers will be obliged to fulfil.
Euro-MPs are expected on Thursday to approve the draft directive, which will for the first time oblige manufacturers to put warning symbols on products which damage the environment.

Other innovations in the proposal include a requirement on manufacturers to provide professional users with safety data for products which are not classed as dangerous -- because they contain only low concentrations of hazardous substances -- but which might present a health risk in use.
Parliament's committee on environment and consumer affairs has already signalled its support for the new directive but will urge Euro-MPs to approve amendments designed to strengthen it.

The amendments may go some small way towards satisfying the three new EU countries -- Austria, Sweden and Finland -- who complain the new directive is not as stringent as their national laws and will force them to accept less well labelled products from other member states.

Among the improvements it is demanding, parliament's environment committee wants products to carry warning symbols when the cumulative total of a product's toxic, corrosive or otherwise dangerous ingredients exceeds a certain level, even when these substances do not individually reach that level.

The directive says product labels must carry not only danger symbols, including a tactile warning for blind people, but also the actual names of all substances which are toxic or cause cancer, mutations or allergies.
Parliament's environment committee also wants labels explicitly to name individual corrosive, irritant and environmentally damaging substances.

But Euro-MPs are not likely to call for labels which list every single hazardous detail of a product, on the grounds that this would confuse users and be too expensive for manufacturers forced to change their packaging.

In addition to its demands on stricter labelling, parliament is expected to insist that toxic products should only be tested on animals for the purpose of hazard classification if there is no alternative test method.
